title: Ultimate concern
hookLine: Paul Tillich: faith is being grasped by what ultimately matters

lines: WHAT WOULD YOU GIVE UP LAST?
cards: What would you give up last? Run down the list slowly: a hobby, a job, a city, money, comfort, your reputation, your plans. Somewhere near the bottom there may be something you'd keep even if all the rest went.
The German theologian Paul Tillich, who later taught in America, said that thing tells you something about faith. Not because it's religious; it might not be.
Because of where it sits in a life: at the bottom of the list, holding everything else up.

teach.b: Tillich's phrase is ultimate concern. Faith, he said, is the state of being grasped by what concerns you ultimately. Notice the verb.
Not grasping: grasped. You don't pick an ultimate concern the way you pick a topping. It takes hold of you, it asks for everything, and it promises, in some way, to fulfill you.
Then he makes an uncomfortable point. Everyone, as Tillich saw it, has something in that place: for one person success, for another a nation, or a person they love.
When what sits there isn't truly ultimate, when it's something finite dressed up as everything, he called it idolatry, and said it ends in disappointment.
Only God, whom he described as the ground of being, can bear that weight.

Some readers connect this with the commandment Jesus called the first: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength." All, and all, and all.

And Jesus said it more plainly still: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Tillich has critics. Some say his language about God grows so abstract it loses the God who speaks and acts in the Bible.
His defenders say he was trying to reach people for whom the old words had gone quiet. Either way, his question cuts close: whatever you'd give up last, can it hold what you're asking it to hold?

how: Tillich is read in seminaries and by thoughtful seekers; some Christians use his question, what concerns me ultimately, as part of an examination of conscience or a retreat.

o: a final verdict on what your life was worth
being grasped by what matters most in a life
the biggest worry keeping you up at night

games.q: what matters most — tap the pairs.
p: Tillich's way of speaking of God

s: for Tillich, only religious people have an ultimate concern
everyone, he said, has something in that place.
Tillich called something finite put in the ultimate place idolatry
and he said it ends in disappointment.
in Tillich's phrase, faith is grasping, not being grasped
faith is being grasped by what concerns you ultimately.

games.q: your job, a nation or a person has become the thing you'd give everything for. what would Tillich ask?
o: can it really bear that weight?
games.why: if something finite sits in the ultimate place, he called it idolatry, and said it ends in disappointment. only God, the ground of being, can bear it.

practice: Ask yourself quietly what you give your best hours to, what you'd sacrifice for, what you're most afraid of losing, and let the honest answer come, even if it surprises you. Hold it gently, without judging it.
If you pray, you can offer that answer to God just as it is.

wordCard.voice: Ultimate concern. Paul Tillich's name for faith: being grasped by what matters ultimately, the thing that asks everything of you.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 6:21: treasure — "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

carryVoice: Your line: what matters most. Grasped, not grasping, by the thing you would give up last. Back tomorrow, same hill.
